rules.quote: Proper nouns always start with capital letters, except for some commercial terms.
rules.specification: The page does not identify the exempt commercial terms. Check their established styling before flagging a lower-case initial.
rules.violation_condition: A proper noun starts with a lower-case letter and is not a commercial term with an established lower-case initial.
when: Applies to names of specific people, organisations, places or things.
Some commercial terms are exceptions.
rules.why: G-4: the body states the actionable capitalisation rule; the heading only defines proper nouns.

covers.quote: They have a capital letter only when they are the first word in a sentence.
Capitalise nouns only if they are part of a proper noun.

parts.quote: The ACT’s Office of the Commissioner for the Environment was the first such agency in Australia.
I worked in the office for 11 years.

rules.quote: Don’t capitalise them if you use them as common nouns.
rules.violation_condition: A noun used generically has a capital initial even though it is not the first word in a sentence or part of a proper noun.
when: Applies when the noun is used as a common noun, including a generic reference to something with a formal name.
A common noun takes a capital initial when it is the first word in a sentence.
Nouns within proper names are outside this prohibition.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: consolidate the repeated prohibition and its sentence-initial exception into one check.

rules.quote: Don’t use an apostrophe before (or after) the ‘s’ to show the plural.
rules.violation_condition: An apostrophe before or after an ‘s’ is used to mark a noun’s plural rather than possession or another legitimate apostrophe use.
when: Applies when the apostrophe is being used to show plurality.
rules.why: G-1 and G-4: use the specific apostrophe instruction, not the descriptive singular-and-plural heading.

rules.quote: A collective noun usually has a singular verb.
rules.violation_condition: A collective noun referring to a group as a whole takes a plural verb.
when: Applies when the collective noun refers to the group as a whole.
The fact that the group contains multiple components does not by itself justify a plural verb.
A plural verb is acceptable when the sentence draws attention to the individual members or parts.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: singular agreement and the individual-members exception are conditions of one check, not separate rules.

covers.quote: Some nouns can be used both ways. The meaning depends on whether the noun is countable or uncountable in the way it is used:

rules.quote: An uncountable noun has no plural and only a singular verb.

when: Applies only when the noun is used in an uncountable sense.

rules.why: The grain test separates plural noun formation from verb agreement; G-2 keeps countable uses as a condition, not another rule.
